### What a static test cannot see {#sec-s2-why-sine}

[S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd) fed the converter a constant and measured
what came back. That finds offset, gain and the noise floor, and it is the
right first experiment — but a constant asks nothing of the converter's
*timing*. A sample taken 10 µs late has exactly the same value as one taken on
time, because the input is not going anywhere.

Put a sinusoid in and every timing error becomes an amplitude error. A sample
taken $\Delta t$ late on a signal with slope $\dot{V}$ reports a voltage wrong
by $\dot{V}\,\Delta t$, and the slope of a sinusoid grows with frequency:

$$
\dot{V}_\max = 2\pi f A
$$ {#eq-s2-slew}

So the same timing error costs ten times as much at 1 kHz as at 100 Hz. That
is the whole experiment: sweep the frequency, watch the effective resolution
fall, and find out where the converter stops being limited by its noise and
starts being limited by its clock.

### The four-parameter sine fit {#sec-s2-fit}

The standard method, from IEEE Std 1057 [@ieee1057] and IEEE Std 1241
[@ieee1241], is to fit a sinusoid to the samples by least squares and study
what is left over. The model is written in the linear-in-parameters form

$$
y_i = A\cos(2\pi f t_i) + B\sin(2\pi f t_i) + C
$$ {#eq-s2-model}

from which the amplitude and phase come out as

$$
\hat{A}_0 = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2},
\qquad
\hat{\varphi} = \operatorname{atan2}(-B,\, A)
$$ {#eq-s2-amp-phase}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Written this way, the fit is *linear* in $A$, $B$ and $C$ for any fixed $f$:
build the design matrix

$$
\mathbf{D} = \begin{bmatrix}
\cos(2\pi f t_0) & \sin(2\pi f t_0) & 1\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
\cos(2\pi f t_{n-1}) & \sin(2\pi f t_{n-1}) & 1
\end{bmatrix}
$$ {#eq-s2-design}

and solve the normal equations
$(\mathbf{D}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{D})\,\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{D}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}$
in one step. That is the **three-parameter** fit, and it is what the standards
specify when the frequency is known exactly.

The **fourth** parameter is $f$ itself, and it is what makes the problem
nonlinear. The standard approach is to iterate: start from a frequency
estimate, take the three-parameter solution at that frequency, and then
improve $f$ by a step that also makes the derivative of the residual with
respect to $f$ vanish. Extending the design matrix with the column

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial f}\left[A\cos(2\pi f t_i) + B\sin(2\pi f t_i)\right]
= 2\pi t_i \left[-A\sin(2\pi f t_i) + B\cos(2\pi f t_i)\right]
$$ {#eq-s2-newton}

and solving the enlarged least-squares problem gives a correction $\Delta f$;
repeating until $\Delta f$ stops changing converges in a handful of steps from
any starting point within a bin or two of the true frequency. The templates
implement exactly this, written out rather than taken from a library, so that
the Python and R versions follow the same arithmetic.

Why fit $f$ at all, when the generator's dial says what it is? Two reasons,
and both are results in their own right. The generator's dial and the
device's clock are two different oscillators, so their ratio is a measurement
(@sec-s2-clock). And a fit at the *wrong* frequency leaves a residual that
looks like distortion and is not, which would corrupt the ENOB.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Coherent and non-coherent sampling {#sec-s2-coherent}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Coherent and non-coherent sampling (1)
:::

If the record contains an exact integer number of signal cycles, and that
integer shares no factor with the number of samples, then the samples land on
$n$ distinct phases spread evenly around the cycle. This is **coherent
sampling**, and it is what the standards ask for: it removes the leakage that
otherwise biases both the fit and any spectral estimate.

The condition is

$$
f = \frac{M}{n}\,f_s, \qquad \gcd(M, n) = 1
$$ {#eq-s2-coherent}

with $M$ the number of cycles in the record and $n$ the number of samples.
Choosing $n$ **prime** makes the coprimality automatic for every $M$ between
$1$ and $n$, which is why the reference data uses $n = 2003$.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Coherent and non-coherent sampling (2)
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Perfect coherence is not available on this platform

@eq-s2-coherent requires knowing $f_s$ exactly, and on a loop-driven sampler
you do not. The records land on `loop()` iterations, so the realised interval
is quantized and the achieved rate differs from the requested one in the last
few digits — S1 measured exactly this. The sweep is therefore *approximately*
coherent, and the fourth parameter is what rescues it: because $f$ is
estimated rather than assumed, a small departure from coherence costs
precision in the frequency estimate rather than biasing the amplitude and the
residual. A three-parameter fit at the nominal frequency would not survive
this, and that is worth knowing before trusting one.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Effective bits, and the two time bases {#sec-s2-enob}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Effective bits, and the two time bases (1)
:::

Subtract the fitted sinusoid and what is left is everything the model does not
explain: noise, quantization, distortion, and timing error. Its RMS,
$\sigma_r$, converts to an effective number of bits exactly as in S1:

$$
\mathrm{ENOB} = \log_2\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{FSR}}{\sqrt{12}\,\sigma_r}\right)
$$ {#eq-s2-enob}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Effective bits, and the two time bases (2)
:::

The experiment computes this **twice from the same samples**, changing only
the time base fed to the fit:

1. with a **uniform grid**, $t_i = t_0 + iT$, which is what you get if you
   assume the converter sampled when it was asked to;
2. with the **device's own `t_us`**, which is when it actually did.

The difference

$$
\Delta_\mathrm{timing} = \mathrm{ENOB}_{t_\mathrm{us}} - \mathrm{ENOB}_\mathrm{uniform}
$$ {#eq-s2-penalty}

is the **timing penalty**, in bits: the resolution you throw away by trusting
the nominal grid. It is the single most useful number this experiment
produces, because it is paid by every acquisition system that reports samples
without timestamps — which is most of them.

### Aperture jitter and the jitter limit {#sec-s2-jitter}

Even with perfect timestamps there is a floor. The sample-and-hold closes at
an instant that is itself uncertain by some $\sigma_j$ — **aperture jitter** —
and that uncertainty is *not* reported in `t_us`, because the device does not
know about it. Through @eq-s2-slew it becomes an amplitude error of standard
deviation $2\pi f A \sigma_j$, and comparing that with the RMS of a full-scale
sinusoid gives the classical limit

$$
\mathrm{SNR}_j = -20\log_{10}\!\left(2\pi f \sigma_j\right)
$$ {#eq-s2-jitter-snr}

which in bits, through the usual $\mathrm{SNR} = 6.02\,\mathrm{ENOB} + 1.76$
dB for a full-scale sinusoid, is

$$
\mathrm{ENOB}_j = \frac{\mathrm{SNR}_j - 1.76}{6.02}
$$ {#eq-s2-jitter-enob}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
@eq-s2-jitter-snr falls at 20 dB per decade of frequency — about 3.3 bits per
decade — while the noise floor measured in S1 is flat. Plot both against
frequency and they cross. Below the crossover the converter is **noise
limited** and a quieter front end helps; above it the converter is **jitter
limited** and only a better clock helps. Knowing which side of that line an
application sits on is the difference between a useful improvement and a
wasted one.

Note also what @eq-s2-jitter-snr does *not* contain: the number of bits. A
16-bit converter and a 12-bit converter with the same aperture jitter reach
the same ceiling at high frequency. Resolution you cannot time is resolution
you do not have.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Clock accuracy {#sec-s2-clock}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Clock accuracy (1)
:::

The fitted frequency $\hat{f}$ is expressed in the device's own time base,
because `t_us` is the device's `micros()`. The generator's frequency
$f_\mathrm{gen}$ is expressed in the generator's. Their ratio is therefore a
comparison of two oscillators:

$$
\delta = \left(\frac{\hat{f}}{f_\mathrm{gen}} - 1\right) \times 10^{6}
\quad [\mathrm{ppm}]
$$ {#eq-s2-ppm}

A device clock running fast makes a given real frequency appear *low* in
device time, so the sign of $\delta$ tells you which way the board's
oscillator errs. The measurement is only ever as good as the generator: its
own frequency uncertainty enters the budget directly, and if the generator is
the worse of the two oscillators, this measures the generator.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Clock accuracy (2)
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The source has to be better than the thing you are measuring

Two requirements, and neither is negotiable.

**The generator's noise and distortion must be below the converter's.** The
residual of the fit cannot tell you whether the imperfection came from the
source or from the converter. If the generator's own harmonic distortion is
$-70$ dB and you are trying to measure an 11-bit converter at $-68$ dB, you
are measuring the generator.

**Never use the board's own DAC as the source.** It shares the reference, the
clock and the ground with the ADC, so its errors are correlated with the ones
you are trying to measure — a gain error in the reference cancels instead of
appearing, and the DAC's own timing jitter is the ADC's jitter. The result
looks excellent and means nothing. Correlated errors are the one failure mode
a residual cannot reveal.
:::

### What S2 hands to the rest of the site {#sec-s2-relation}

S1 measured the noise floor with a constant input; that is the **upper bound**
this experiment's dynamic ENOB approaches at low frequency, and comparing the
two is the first check that both experiments were done correctly. The
crossover frequency of @sec-s2-jitter tells [S3](../S3-aliasing-filtering/index.qmd)
how much of its filter design budget is worth spending, and it tells M3
whether a modal peak can be resolved at all.
